claim: Sleep and feeding patterns lack strong daily rhythms during early life in diurnal animals.
source: Sleep and feeding patterns lack strong daily rhythms during early life.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about diurnal animals during early development.

claim: As diurnal animals mature, feeding is consolidated to the day and sleep to the night.
source: As diurnal animals mature, feeding is consolidated to the day and sleep to the night.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general developmental pattern.

claim: In Drosophila, circadian sleep patterns are initiated with formation of a circuit connecting the central clock to arousal output neurons.
source: In Drosophila, circadian sleep patterns are initiated with formation of a circuit connecting the central clock to arousal output neurons
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about Drosophila development.

claim: Emergence of circadian sleep enables long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila larvae.
source: emergence of circadian sleep also enables long-term memory (LTM).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a consequence of circadian sleep emergence.

claim: In the 2nd instar larval period (L2), sleep and feeding are spread across the day.
source: We find that in the 2nd instar larval period (L2), sleep and feeding are spread across the day
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Sleep and feeding behaviors become organized into daily patterns by the 3rd instar larval stage (L3).
source: these behaviors become organized into daily patterns by the 3rd instar larval stage (L3).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Forcing mature (L3) animals to adopt immature (L2) feeding strategies disrupts sleep-wake rhythms.
source: Forcing mature (L3) animals to adopt immature (L2) feeding strategies disrupts sleep-wake rhythms
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from experimental manipulation.

claim: Forcing mature (L3) animals to adopt immature (L2) feeding strategies disrupts the ability to exhibit LTM.
source: Forcing mature (L3) animals to adopt immature (L2) feeding strategies disrupts sleep-wake rhythms and the ability to exhibit LTM.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from experimental manipulation.

claim: The development of the clock (DN1a)-arousal (Dh44) circuit is influenced by the larval nutritional environment.
source: In addition, the development of the clock (DN1a)-arousal (Dh44) circuit itself is influenced by the larval nutritional environment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Larval arousal Dh44 neurons act through glucose metabolic genes to drive onset of daily sleep-wake rhythms.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that larval arousal Dh44 neurons act through glucose metabolic genes to drive onset of daily sleep-wake rhythms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Changes to energetic demands in developing organisms trigger the formation of sleep-circadian circuits and behaviors.
source: Together, our data suggest that changes to energetic demands in developing organisms trigger the formation of sleep-circadian circuits and behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The development of behavioral rhythms such as sleep-wake patterns is critical for brain development.
source: The development of behavioral rhythms such as sleep-wake patterns is critical for brain development (Vallone et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Early life circadian disruptions in rodents negatively impacts adult behaviors, neuronal morphology, and circadian physiology.
source: Indeed, early life circadian disruptions in rodents negatively impacts adult behaviors, neuronal morphology, and circadian physiology (Varcoe et al., 2016; Mendez et al., 2016; Ameen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Disruptions in sleep and rhythms during development are a common co-morbidity in neurodevelopmental disorders including ADHD and autism.
source: Likewise, in humans, disruptions in sleep and rhythms during development are a common co-morbidity in neurodevelopmental disorders including ADHD and autism (Hoffmire et al., 2014; Krakowiak et al., 2008; Kotagal, 2015; Ednick et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: L2 larvae show no differences in feeding rate across the day.
source: While we observed no differences in feeding rate across the day in L2
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: L3 larvae show diurnal differences in feeding with higher feeding rate during the subjective day compared to the subjective night.
source: we found that L3 show diurnal differences in feeding with higher feeding rate during the subjective day compared to the subjective night (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: L2 larvae consume the same amount at CT1 and CT13.
source: Analysis of total food intake indicated that L2 consume the same amount at CT1 and CT13
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: L3 larvae consume more at CT1 than at CT13.
source: however, L3 consume more at CT1 than at CT13 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The daily feeding pattern in L3 requires a functioning molecular clock.
source: We observed no differences in feeding rate across the day in L3 tim mutants indicating that the daily feeding pattern requires a functioning molecular clock (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C showing tim mutants lack feeding rhythms.

claim: L3 raised on low sugar (L.S.) food show feeding spread out across the day similar to L2 on normal food.
source: We found that the feeding pattern in L3 raised on L.S. food closely resembled that of L2 on normal food (8% glucose), with feeding spread out across the day (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: L3 raised on low sugar food lose diurnal differences in sleep duration compared to L3 raised on control food.
source: Compared to L3 raised on control food, this paradigm was also associated with loss of diurnal differences in sleep duration, sleep bout number, and arousal threshold (indicating less deep sleep) (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: L3 raised on low sugar food lose diurnal differences in sleep bout number compared to L3 raised on control food.
source: Compared to L3 raised on control food, this paradigm was also associated with loss of diurnal differences in sleep duration, sleep bout number, and arousal threshold (indicating less deep sleep) (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: L3 raised on low sugar food show less deep sleep (higher arousal threshold) compared to L3 raised on control food.
source: Compared to L3 raised on control food, this paradigm was also associated with loss of diurnal differences in sleep duration, sleep bout number, and arousal threshold (indicating less deep sleep) (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of NPF+ neurons stimulates feeding in L3.
source: Next, to avoid chronic effects of this dietary manipulation, we acutely stimulated feeding in L3 reared on normal food using thermogenetic activation of NPF +neurons (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Wu et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Enforcing a constant feeding pattern through NPF+ neuron activation leads to loss of sleep rhythms in L3.
source: Like L.S. conditions, enforcing a constant feeding pattern through NPF +neuron activation led to loss of sleep rhythms and loss of deep sleep (higher arousal threshold) in L3 (Figure 2B–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Enforcing a constant feeding pattern through NPF+ neuron activation leads to loss of deep sleep in L3.
source: Like L.S. conditions, enforcing a constant feeding pattern through NPF +neuron activation led to loss of sleep rhythms and loss of deep sleep (higher arousal threshold) in L3 (Figure 2B–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: NPF+ neuron activation in L3 results in loss of long-term memory.
source: Consistent with deeper sleep stages being necessary for LTM, we observed a loss of LTM in either the NPF +neuron activation (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: L3 raised on low sugar conditions show loss of long-term memory.
source: we observed a loss of LTM in either the NPF +neuron activation (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–I) or under L.S. conditions (Figure 2H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2H.

claim: Short-term memory (STM) is intact in L3 with NPF+ neuron activation.
source: short-term memory (STM) was intact in both manipulations (Figure 2G and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2G.

claim: Short-term memory (STM) is intact in L3 raised on low sugar conditions.
source: short-term memory (STM) was intact in both manipulations (Figure 2G and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2I.

claim: Gaboxadol feeding induces deeper sleep in L2 as reflected by an increase in arousal threshold.
source: Gaboxadol feeding induced deeper sleep in L2 (as reflected by an increase in arousal threshold) although sleep duration was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Gaboxadol feeding does not change sleep duration in L2.
source: Gaboxadol feeding induced deeper sleep in L2 (as reflected by an increase in arousal threshold) although sleep duration was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Despite achieving deeper sleep with gaboxadol, LTM is still not evident in L2.
source: Despite achieving deeper sleep, LTM was still not evident in L2 (Figure 3A, B and E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: L2 on gaboxadol fail to develop normally.
source: however, in contrast to L3, L2 on gaboxadol failed to develop normally (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Acute activation of sleep-inducing neurons causes an increase in sleep duration in L2.
source: We found that acute activation of these neurons caused an increase in sleep duration and bout length with a decrease in arousal threshold (Figure 3F and G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Acute activation of sleep-inducing neurons causes an increase in bout length in L2.
source: We found that acute activation of these neurons caused an increase in sleep duration and bout length with a decrease in arousal threshold (Figure 3F and G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Acute activation of sleep-inducing neurons causes a decrease in arousal threshold in L2.
source: We found that acute activation of these neurons caused an increase in sleep duration and bout length with a decrease in arousal threshold (Figure 3F and G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Inducing deeper sleep in L2 via genetic approaches does not improve LTM performance.
source: However, inducing deeper sleep in L2 via genetic approaches likewise did not improve LTM performance (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–K)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: Short-term memory is intact in L2 with thermogenetic induction of deeper sleep.
source: despite STM being intact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Thermogenetic induction of deeper sleep stages disrupts larval development in L2.
source: Moreover, as with gaboxadol feeding in L2, thermogenetic induction of deeper sleep stages disrupted larval development (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Activation of DN1as in L3 raised on control food causes an increase in calcium in Dh44 neurons.
source: As expected, activation of DN1as in L3 raised on control food caused an increase in calcium in Dh44 neurons (Figure 4A and B; Poe et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A and B.

claim: In L3 raised on low sugar conditions, activation of DN1as does not elicit a response in Dh44 neurons.
source: In contrast, in L3 raised on L.S. conditions, activation of DN1as no longer elicited a response in Dh44 neurons (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: CCHa1 peptide application increases intracellular calcium in Dh44 neurons in early L3.
source: As anticipated, we observed an increase in intracellular calcium in early L3 (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: CCHa1 application does not alter calcium levels in Dh44 neurons in L2.
source: surprisingly, CCHa1 application did not alter calcium levels in Dh44 neurons in L2 (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: Dh44 neurons are not capable of receiving CCHa1 input prior to early L3.
source: CCHa1 application did not alter calcium levels in Dh44 neurons in L2 (Figure 4F), indicating that Dh44 neurons are not capable of receiving CCHa1 input prior to early L3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data in Figure 4F.

claim: CCHa1 application in L3 reared on low sugar fails to elicit a response in Dh44 neurons.
source: Moreover, CCHa1 application in L3 reared on L.S. also failed to elicit a response in Dh44 neurons (Figure 4G)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Sub-optimal nutritional milieu influences the development of Dh44 neuronal competency to receive clock-driven cues.
source: CCHa1 application in L3 reared on L.S. also failed to elicit a response in Dh44 neurons (Figure 4G) suggesting that sub-optimal nutritional milieu influences the development of Dh44 neuronal competency to receive clock-driven cues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data in Figure 4G.

claim: Knockdown of Glut1 in Dh44 neurons results in loss of rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3.
source: We found that knockdown of glucose metabolism genes, Glut1, Hex-C and PyK, in Dh44 neurons resulted in a loss of rhythmic changes in sleep duration and bout number (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Knockdown of Hex-C in Dh44 neurons results in loss of rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3.
source: We found that knockdown of glucose metabolism genes, Glut1, Hex-C and PyK, in Dh44 neurons resulted in a loss of rhythmic changes in sleep duration and bout number (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of PyK in Dh44 neurons results in loss of rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3.
source: We found that knockdown of glucose metabolism genes, Glut1, Hex-C and PyK, in Dh44 neurons resulted in a loss of rhythmic changes in sleep duration and bout number (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of Hex-C in Dh44 neurons has no effect on L3 feeding.
source: with no effect on L3 feeding in the Hex-C manipulation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockdown of Hex-C in DN1as does not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3.
source: Additionally, knockdown of Hex-C in DN1as did not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Manipulation of glucose metabolic genes in L2 does not affect sleep duration at CT1 and CT13.
source: Manipulation of glucose metabolic genes in L2 did not affect sleep duration at CT1 and CT13 (Figure 5E–G; Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–O)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Knockdown of Gcn2 in Dh44 neurons does not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3.
source: In contrast to their role in adult Dh44 neurons, knockdown of amino acid sensing genes, Gcn2 and crc, in Dh44 neurons did not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration and bout number in L3 (Figure 5H and I; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5H.

claim: Knockdown of crc in Dh44 neurons does not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration in L3.
source: In contrast to their role in adult Dh44 neurons, knockdown of amino acid sensing genes, Gcn2 and crc, in Dh44 neurons did not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration and bout number in L3 (Figure 5H and I; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5I.

claim: Dh44 neurons may not act through amino acid sensing pathways to regulate sleep-wake rhythm development.
source: knockdown of amino acid sensing genes, Gcn2 and crc, in Dh44 neurons did not disrupt rhythmic changes in sleep duration and bout number in L3 (Figure 5H and I; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D) suggesting that Dh44 neurons may not act through amino acid sensing pathways to regulate sleep-wake rhythm development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data in Figure 5H and I.

claim: Dh44 neurons require glucose metabolic genes to drive sleep-wake rhythm development.
source: Thus, Dh44 neurons require glucose metabolic genes to drive sleep-wake rhythm development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the glucose metabolism gene knockdown experiments.

claim: The low sugar dietary paradigm did not affect any measures of larval growth or development.
source: Critically, this paradigm did not affect any measures of larval growth or development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: In adult Drosophila, sleep and feeding behaviors are consolidated to specific times of day with flies eating more in the day than the night.
source: In adult Drosophila, sleep and feeding behaviors are consolidated to specific times of day with flies eating more in the day than the night (Barber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Sleep in 2nd instar Drosophila larvae (L2) lacks a circadian pattern.
source: Yet, early in development, sleep in 2nd instar Drosophila larvae (L2) lacks a circadian pattern (Poe et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Sleep-wake rhythms are initiated in early 3rd instar Drosophila larvae (L3) at 72 hr AEL.
source: We previously determined that sleep-wake rhythms are initiated in early 3rd instar Drosophila larvae (L3) (72 hr AEL).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: DN1a clock neurons anatomically and functionally connect to Dh44 arousal output neurons to drive the consolidation of sleep in L3.
source: DN1a clock neurons anatomically and functionally connect to Dh44 arousal output neurons to drive the consolidation of sleep in L3.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Development of the DN1a-Dh44 circuit promotes deeper sleep in L3 resulting in the emergence of long-term memory (LTM) capabilities at the L3 stage but not before.
source: Development of this circuit promotes deeper sleep in L3 resulting in the emergence of long-term memory (LTM) capabilities at the L3 stage but not before (Poe et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Early in development, most young animals must obtain enough nutrients to ensure proper growth.
source: Early in development, most young animals must obtain enough nutrients to ensure proper growth (Ghosh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Developing organisms must sleep to support nervous system development.
source: Yet, developing organisms must also sleep to support nervous system development (Vallone et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Conflicting needs (feeding vs. quiescence) result in rapid transitions between sleeping and feeding states early in life.
source: These conflicting needs (feeding vs. quiescence) result in rapid transitions between sleeping and feeding states early in life (Adair and Bauchner, 1993; Levin and Stern, 1975).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: As development proceeds, nutritional intake and storage capacity increase, allowing for the consolidation of feeding and sleep to specific times of day.
source: As development proceeds, nutritional intake and storage capacity increase, allowing for the consolidation of feeding and sleep to specific times of day (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Mammalian body composition and nutritional capacity change over infant development.
source: These changes in nutritional storage capacity are likely conserved as mammalian body composition and nutritional capacity change over infant development (Toro-Ramos et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Drosophila show rapid increases in overall larval body size including the size of the fat body (used for nutrient storage) across development.
source: and Drosophila show rapid increases in overall larval body size including the size of the fat body (used for nutrient storage) across development (Butterworth et al., 1988; Jacobs et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: In adult Drosophila, Dh44 neurons act as nutrient sensors to regulate food consumption and starvation-induced sleep suppression through the activity of both glucose and amino acid sensing genes.
source: In adult Drosophila, Dh44 neurons act as nutrient sensors to regulate food consumption and starvation-induced sleep suppression through the activity of both glucose and amino acid sensing genes (Dus et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021; Oh and Suh, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Dh44 neurons are activated by changes in bath application of nutritive sugars.
source: Indeed, Dh44 neurons themselves are activated by changes in bath application of nutritive sugars (Dus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Disruption to circadian sleep and/or to deeper sleep stages during development is associated with impairments in long-term memory formation.
source: Disruption to circadian sleep and/or to deeper sleep stages during development is associated with impairments in long-term memory formation (Ameen et al., 2022; Konrad et al., 2016; Seehagen et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2019; Smarr et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Deeper sleep stages are necessary for long-term memory.
source: Consistent with deeper sleep stages being necessary for LTM, we observed a loss of LTM in either the NPF +neuron activation (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–I) or under L.S. conditions (Figure 2H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I)
evidence: This is implied by the phrase 'Consistent with deeper sleep stages being necessary for LTM' and supported by the experimental results showing loss of LTM when deep sleep is disrupted.

claim: Sleep cannot be leveraged to enhance cognitive function prematurely because prolonged periods of deep sleep are not energetically sustainable at the L2 stage.
source: These data suggest that sleep cannot be leveraged to enhance cognitive function prematurely because prolonged periods of deep sleep are not energetically sustainable at this stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data showing that inducing deep sleep in L2 disrupts development without improving LTM.

claim: The nascent connection underlying circadian sleep in Drosophila is developmentally plastic.
source: Thus, the nascent connection underlying circadian sleep in Drosophila is developmentally plastic: in an insufficient nutritional environment, this connection is not functional, presumably to facilitate a more constant feeding pattern that fulfills energetic needs of the animal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data showing that the DN1a-Dh44 connection is disrupted under low sugar conditions.

claim: In an insufficient nutritional environment, the DN1a-Dh44 connection is not functional to facilitate a more constant feeding pattern that fulfills energetic needs of the animal.
source: Thus, the nascent connection underlying circadian sleep in Drosophila is developmentally plastic: in an insufficient nutritional environment, this connection is not functional, presumably to facilitate a more constant feeding pattern that fulfills energetic needs of the animal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The constant feeding pattern under low nutrient conditions eschews deep sleep at the expense of LTM.
source: However, this feeding pattern eschews deep sleep at the expense of LTM.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Release of CCHamide-1 (CCHa1) from DN1as to CCHa1mide-1 receptor (CCHa1-R) on Dh44 neurons is necessary for sleep-wake rhythms in L3.
source: We previously determined that release of CCHamide-1 (CCHa1) from DN1as to CCHa1mide-1 receptor (CCHa1-R) on Dh44 neurons is necessary for sleep-wake rhythms in L3 (Poe et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Dh44 neurons are poised to receive clock (DN1a) input as soon the connection forms between these cellular populations.
source: Our data support a model in which the downstream Dh44 neurons are poised to receive clock (DN1a) input as soon the connection forms between these cellular populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a model based on the data.

claim: The nutritional environment influences DN1a-Dh44 circuit development.
source: Thus, our data indicate that the nutritional environment influences DN1a-Dh44 circuit development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Nutritional environment and energetic status exert profound effects on sleep patterns during development.
source: Nutritional environment and energetic status exert profound effects on sleep patterns during development, but mechanisms coupling sleep to these factors remain undefined.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a general statement.

claim: The development of sleep-circadian circuits depends on organisms achieving sufficient nutritional status to support the consolidation of deep sleep at night.
source: We report that the development of sleep-circadian circuits depends on organisms achieving sufficient nutritional status to support the consolidation of deep sleep at night (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main finding of the study.

claim: Larval Dh44 neurons require glucose metabolic genes but not amino acid sensing genes to modulate sleep-wake rhythms.
source: Our data demonstrate that larval Dh44 neurons require glucose metabolic genes but not amino acid sensing genes to modulate sleep-wake rhythms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main finding of the study.

claim: Larval Dh44 neurons may have distinct functions from their adult counterparts for integrating information about the nutritional environment through the direct sensing of glucose levels to modulate sleep-wake rhythm development.
source: Larval Dh44 neurons may therefore have distinct functions from their adult counterparts for integrating information about the nutritional environment through the direct sensing of glucose levels to modulate sleep-wake rhythm development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Maintaining energy homeostasis and sensing of the nutritional environment are likely conserved regulators of sleep-wake rhythm development.
source: Maintaining energy homeostasis and sensing of the nutritional environment are likely conserved regulators of sleep-wake rhythm development, as young mice exposed to a maternal low-protein diet show disruptions in night-time sleep architecture and energy expenditure later in life (Sutton et al., 2010; Crossland et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation support.

claim: Young mice exposed to a maternal low-protein diet show disruptions in night-time sleep architecture and energy expenditure later in life.
source: as young mice exposed to a maternal low-protein diet show disruptions in night-time sleep architecture and energy expenditure later in life (Sutton et al., 2010; Crossland et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation support.

claim: Changes in both overall circuit development and molecular changes in post-synaptic (Dh44) neurons likely drive sleep-wake rhythm circuit development.
source: Together with our previously published work, our findings support a model in which changes in both overall circuit development and molecular changes in post-synaptic (Dh44) neurons likely drive sleep-wake rhythm circuit development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a model based on the data.

claim: Dh44 neurons may undergo changes in CCHa1-R expression or subcellular localization between the L2 and L3 stages.
source: Our CCHa1 peptide data suggest that Dh44 neurons may undergo changes in CCHa1-R expression or subcellular localization between the L2 and L3 stages
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the CCHa1 peptide data.

claim: The larval nutritional environment may modulate CCHa1-R localization or expression.
source: Interestingly, this increase in activity is absent in low nutrient conditions (Figure 4G) suggesting that the larval nutritional environment may also modulate CCHa1-R localization or expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data in Figure 4G.

claim: Larval Dh44 neurons may respond to an increase in glucose levels in the environment by promoting CCHa1-R localization to the membrane.
source: Perhaps larval Dh44 neurons respond to an increase in glucose levels in the environment by promoting CCHa1-R localization to the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative model.

claim: Changes in CCHa1-R subcellular localization allow Dh44 neurons to become competent to receive clock-driven cues.
source: In this model, changes in CCHa1-R subcellular localization allow Dh44 neurons to become competent to receive clock-driven cues, while this or other Dh44-derived signals promote circuit connectivity with DN1as to drive consolidation of sleep at the L3 stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative model.

claim: Larvae exhibit both sleep-wake and feeding daily rhythms at the L3 stage, but not earlier.
source: Our findings demonstrate that larvae exhibit both sleep-wake and feeding daily rhythms at the L3 stage, but not earlier (Poe et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation support.

claim: Knockdown of Hex-C in Dh44 neurons disrupts sleep rhythms with no obvious effect on feeding behavior.
source: For example, knockdown of Hex-C in Dh44 neurons disrupts sleep rhythms with no obvious effect on feeding behavior (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Sleep and feeding are highly inter-connected behaviors.
source: It is, of course, possible to affect both sleep and feeding behaviors with the same manipulation (e.g. activation of NPF +neurons) underscoring that they are highly inter-connected behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.
